title: Schedule
solution_outline: P1: Normalize a complete block by making one week all 1; the remaining member-2 supports must be an intersecting antichain.

nodes.name: Four patterns mean all coworkers meet
nodes.statement: Represent each team by its attendance column. Two teams' four cross-team pairs all meet exactly when their two columns exhibit 11, 12, 21, and 22. Company isolation is infinite exactly when some pair of columns misses one of these patterns.
nodes.accept: Translate each pair of attending members into one of the four ordered attendance patterns. The relevant pairs are people from different teams, not the two members of one team.

nodes.name: Isolation equals sliding block coverage
nodes.statement: For 1 <= d <= w, isolation is at most d exactly when every consecutive d-week block exhibits all four patterns for every pair of teams. Any finite isolation is at most w.
nodes.accept: A missing meeting in a d-week window creates a gap exceeding d, with virtual endpoints 0 and w+1. Conversely, the first and last d-week windows bound endpoint gaps, and intermediate windows bound consecutive-meeting gaps.

nodes.name: Normalize columns into intersecting antichains
nodes.statement: A complete t-week block can be normalized by independently swapping each team's member labels so its first row is all 1. The member-2 supports on the remaining t-1 weeks then form an intersecting antichain: distinct supports intersect and neither contains the other. This characterization is reversible.
nodes.accept: Label swaps permute the four required patterns. The first row supplies 11; intersection supplies 22; the two nonempty set differences supply 12 and 21. Thus complete blocks correspond to intersecting antichains after normalization.

nodes.name: Intersecting antichain capacity bound
nodes.statement: For t >= 4, a complete t-week block has at most binomial(t-1, floor((t-1)/2)+1) teams. This follows from Milner's theorem: an intersecting antichain on m elements has size at most binomial(m, floor(m/2)+1).
nodes.accept: Apply the intersecting-antichain theorem to the t-1 remaining weeks. Equivalent exact extremal bounds for binary strength-two covering arrays count. Ordinary Sperner's theorem alone is insufficient when t-1 is even.

nodes.name: Upper-middle subsets attain capacity
nodes.statement: On m=t-1 weeks, all subsets of size floor(m/2)+1 form an intersecting antichain. Choosing any n distinct such subsets as member-2 supports, and adding an all-1 week, constructs a complete t-week block whenever n does not exceed their binomial count.
nodes.accept: Two chosen supports intersect because their sizes sum to more than m. Equal size and distinctness give both nonempty differences. The extra all-1 row supplies the remaining pattern. Supports may be enumerated as fixed-popcount masks; their order is irrelevant.

nodes.name: Repeat a shortest complete block
nodes.statement: Let t >= 4 be smallest with binomial(t-1, floor((t-1)/2)+1) >= n. If w<t, output infinity. Otherwise output t and repeat a complete t-week block formed from an all-1 week and n distinct ceil(t/2)-subset member-2 supports on the remaining weeks.
nodes.accept: Every t-week window in the periodic schedule is a cyclic rotation of a complete block, including boundary windows. Smaller isolation implies a shorter complete block, contradicting the capacity bound; fewer than four weeks cannot contain four patterns. For n<=10000, t<=17; scanning up to 2^(t-1) masks and printing nw characters fits the limits. Permuting block rows or team columns preserves correctness.

end.statement: A solver holding every node of one END route can write a correct, fast enough program by routine coding; each route is an approach whose program the judge accepted.

hazards.statement: The endpoint gaps use virtual weeks 0 and w+1, not weeks 1 and w; a finite schedule must satisfy both endpoint bounds as well as internal gaps.
hazards.check: Check the first meeting is at most the reported isolation and the final meeting is at least w+1 minus that isolation, or establish coverage of every window of the reported length.

hazards.statement: Finite output requires exactly w attendance strings of length n, containing only 1 and 2. Impossible output is the single word infinity.
hazards.check: Ensure the block is repeated or truncated to exactly w rows, every row has one character per team, and no schedule is printed after infinity.

hazards.statement: Capacity computations must avoid overflow; binomial coefficients for up to 52 weeks can exceed 32-bit integers.
hazards.check: Use 64-bit binomial arithmetic, saturate at n, or stop computation early enough to prove all intermediate values fit.

paths.approach: Normalize a complete block by making one week all 1; the remaining member-2 supports must be an intersecting antichain. Milner's theorem bounds their number, and taking all subsets just larger than half the remaining weeks attains that bound. Repeat the shortest sufficiently large block: every window of one period covers all meetings, and no smaller isolation could avoid the complete-block lower bound.
paths.notes: The earlier constructions also satisfy the stated four-pattern and endpoint conditions. This version enumerates fixed-popcount supports by increasing numeric mask, with high bits printed first; this is an optional ordering, not a new mathematical claim.

exploration.reason: The accepted path gives the exact extremal capacity and an optimal schedule for every input. I found no additional approach with both a genuinely different output construction and a justified worst-case running time within the limits.
considered: Binary team identifiers followed by complemented rows can ensure meetings, but generally require more weeks than the exact optimum.
Searching for a maximum clique among pairwise compatible attendance columns is an equivalent exact formulation, but its exponential search is not justified for up to 10000 teams.
Randomized covering-array generation does not guarantee finding an optimal block or proving impossibility.

Complementing all member labels, choosing supports containing a distinguished week, permuting rows, and changing combination enumeration are equivalent forms of the accepted subset construction, not new paths.
Alternative extremal proofs and complementary-pair counting for even block lengths establish the same capacity and construction claims rather than a separate complete approach.
